articles.title: A jornada da mulher que levou o namorado à prisão por transmitir HIV  | G1
articles.standfirst: Jean foi condenado a cinco anos de prisão no regime semiaberto; ele ainda responde a outros processos pelo mesmo crime. Novas vítimas podem procurar acolhimento no Ministério Público de Rondônia.
articles.summary: Jean foi condenado a cinco anos de prisão e ao pagamento de uma indenização de R$ 50 mil à vítima; ele ainda responde a outros processos pelo mesmo crime.
articles.body:
Maria* tinha rotina ativa de exercícios físicos que foi abruptamente interrompida por febres, dores intensas e um cansaço inexplicável. A rápida perda de saúde foi o primeiro sinal de uma violência silenciosa praticada dentro de sua própria casa: ela foi infectada propositalmente com o vírus HIV pelo então namorado , o dentista Jean José Dunga, de 41 anos, morador de Porto Velho.

"Com certeza posso afirmar que foi o momento mais triste e mais difícil da minha vida", lamenta.

*Para proteger a identidade da vítima, que teme o estigma social e a exposição de sua família, ela será identificada nesta reportagem pelo nome fictício de Maria. A identidade do acusado é real.

➡️ O diagnóstico resultou em um inquérito policial e, posteriormente, em uma denúncia à Justiça. Em agosto, Jean recebeu uma pena de cinco anos e também foi condenado a pagar uma indenização de R$ 50 mil à vítima, com possibilidade de recorrer da decisão. Ele responde ainda a outros processos pela mesma acusação.

O acusado foi preso no dia 10 de junho, mas passou a cumprir a pena em regime semiaberto após a condenação. Nesta semana o Ministério Público de Rondônia (MP-RO) pediu à Justiça uma nova prisão preventiva em regime fechado alegando o risco iminente de novas contaminações. O pedido foi acatado na quarta-feira (9). e

🔎 As investigações contra o réu nasceram a partir dos acolhimentos feitos nas salas do Núcleo de Atendimento às Vítimas (Navit) do MP-RO. O órgão acusou Jean de transmitir intencionalmente o vírus HIV a pelo menos quatro mulheres e afirma que é possível que existam outras vítimas ainda não diagnosticadas.

Jean José Dunga de Oliveira — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal/Vítima

Maria e Jean se conheceram em um site de relacionamentos e rapidamente começaram a namorar. Ela conta que ele era gentil, agradável, estava sempre de bom humor e tinha muitas histórias para contar. A forte conexão fazia com que passassem muito tempo juntos.

Mas o "paraíso" durou pouco. Os sintomas do vírus apareceram rapidamente: infecções que não passavam mesmo com uso de antibiótico, dores no corpo, vermelhidão, coceira, dor de cabeça e cansaço.

"O Jean falou que ele poderia me prescrever o antibiótico, que não precisava contar pra ninguém da minha família que a infecção não havia passado, mas isso me acendeu uma pequena luz", relata a vítima.

Como os sintomas só aumentavam, a mulher decidiu fazer exames com a intenção de descartar infecções sexualmente transmissíveis. Para sua surpresa, veio o resultado positivo para HIV.

Naquele momento Maria ainda não sabia, mas o Ministério Público investigava Jean há cerca de quatro meses e ela não era a primeira vítima; ele respondia a uma ação penal envolvendo outras três mulheres. O órgão disparou um alerta para as unidades de saúde e foi assim que ela descobriu o crime: ao buscar atendimento com uma infectologista.

"Ao me perguntarem o nome do meu antigo parceiro, correspondia ao do suspeito; se tratava da mesma pessoa. Eu era mais uma vítima do Jean", relembra.

O choque de descobrir que o homem com quem dividia a vida já era um alvo das autoridades transformou a dor em indignação.

"Além de eu estar com uma doença incurável, fui contaminada de forma intencional, ou seja, de forma criminosa, por uma pessoa que havia usufruído de toda intimidade da minha casa e família, e pessoa que conhecia todas as minhas comorbidades e problemas emocionais", lamenta.

"Quando fui infectada pelo Jean, ele não adoeceu somente a mim, ele adoeceu uma família inteira. Há um luto, ele atingiu todas as pessoas que me amam e estão ao meu lado", complementa.

A denúncia do MP-RO contra Jean aponta que ele tem conhecimento do próprio diagnóstico há cerca de 10 anos e optou por não aderir ao tratamento antirretroviral. A hipótese é que o homem não quis se tratar justamente para transmitir o vírus às pessoas com quem se relacionava.

🔎 O tratamento feito corretamente mantém a carga viral indetectável e impede a transmissão.

Em busca de assistência e justiça, Maria compareceu ao Navit no dia 28 de maio. O espaço, que funciona na sede do Ministério Público de Rondônia, é estruturado para oferecer um ambiente de acolhimento especializado, sigiloso e humanizado para vítimas de violência.

"Estava doendo, mas eu iria fazer o que tivesse que fazer. Ele poderia enfrentar a impunidade de outras pessoas e de outras vítimas, mas da minha parte jamais ele terá impunidade", afirma Maria sobre a decisão de buscar as autoridades.

Os relatos da vítima foram fundamentais para a prisão de Jean no dia 10 de junho. Segundo o MP-RO, o pedido foi feito porque ficou evidente que, mesmo respondendo à primeira ação penal, o homem continuava se relacionando com outras mulheres e transmitindo o vírus.

" Terminei o namoro com ele no dia 30 de abril e a prisão ocorreu somente em 10 de junho. Nesse lapso temporal, ele foi visto saindo com duas moças diferentes. Não posso afirmar que eram namoradas, mas infelizmente ele teve tempo suficiente pra fazer novas vítimas", alerta Maria.

➡️ Mais de )quatro vítimas de Jean foram acolhidas no Navit. Segundo o MP-RO, as mulheres narraram sentimentos de medo, culpa, vergonha, sofrimento emocional, ansiedade e preocupação com a exposição de sua condição de saúde. Uma delas chegou a relatar que demorou a pedir ajuda por medo do julgamento social.

O MP-RO acusou Jean por lesão corporal gravíssima e perigo de contágio de doença grave. Para duas das mulheres, ele também foi acusado de estupro.

Diante da gravidade e da repetição sistemática dos crimes, o órgão pediu que o réu seja obrigado a arcar com todos os custos médicos e psicológicos das vítimas e que ressarça o Sistema Único de Saúde (SUS) pelos gastos gerados com os tratamentos.

O primeiro caso a ser julgado foi o de Maria. Em 24 de agosto, Jean foi condenado a cinco anos de prisão em regime semiaberto e passou a cumprir a pena em uma colônia penal de Porto Velho. No entanto, outros dois processos contra ele ainda tramitam na Justiça. Após a condenação, o MP-RO pediu uma nova prisão preventiva, alegando risco iminente de novas vítimas. Na quarta-feira (9), o acusado voltou a ser preso.

Antes da condenação, a defesa de Jean prestou solidariedade às vítimas e afirmou ao g1 que o acusado realizava tratamento antirretroviral e acreditava não haver risco de transmissão sexual do HIV. Após a condenação, a reportagem voltou a procurar o advogado, que optou por não se pronunciar.

De acordo com a infectologista Mariana Vasconcelos, o maior inimigo de quem convive com o vírus hoje não é a doença em si, mas a desinformação e o preconceito. Um peso que é sentido na pele por quem é diagnosticado.

"Não posso me identificar sem sofrer prejuízos ou expor familiares a prejuízo social. Infelizmente, a sociedade ainda cobra um preço para esse tipo de contágio, ainda há um grande tabu social e as pessoas são muito cruéis com comentários às vítimas", reforça Maria.

No entanto, a especialista explica que, com o avanço da medicina, o diagnóstico precoce é o passaporte para uma rotina saudável. O tratamento feito corretamente torna a pessoa indetectável e intransmissível.

"Hoje em dia, o tratamento base no Brasil é feito com apenas dois comprimidos diários, que praticamente não têm efeitos colaterais. O paciente que faz o diagnóstico de forma precoce e toma a medicação direitinho tem uma expectativa de vida que se assemelha à da população geral", tranquiliza a médica.

Qualquer pessoa que desconfie ter sido exposta ao vírus pode procurar as Unidades Básicas de Saúde (UBS) ou UPAs para realizar o teste rápido de forma gratuita e sigilosa. Para quem tem muito medo da exposição inicial, existe também a opção do autoteste, que pode ser comprado em farmácias.

Caso haja a confirmação do diagnóstico, as vítimas em Rondônia podem procurar o Núcleo de Atendimento às Vítimas (Navit) pelos telefones:

O espaço é preparado para lidar com situações de vulnerabilidade e os responsáveis são compromissados em conciliar a apuração dos fatos com o cuidado necessário à privacidade das vítimas.

"O Navit atua como porta de entrada da rede de proteção às vítimas, oferecendo um ambiente seguro, acolhedor e especializado para escuta, orientação e encaminhamento. Esse trabalho possibilita que mulheres em situação de violência relatem experiências extremamente sensíveis com segurança e confiança", reforça o MP-RO.

As vítimas também podem procurar as Delegacias Especializadas de Atendimento à Mulher (Deam) ou outras unidades da Polícia Civil ou Militar.

Diante da possibilidade real de existirem outras mulheres infectadas na região, a própria Maria deixa um apelo final para que o silêncio seja rompido:

"Não se sinta culpada. Parece o fim do mundo, mas não é. Procure ajuda no Navit ou nas delegacias especializadas. Que vocês saibam que não estão sozinhas nessa luta; tem muita gente nos bastidores que faz a justiça acontecer".

articles.title: Potencial de terras raras pode colocar Amapá no radar internacional | G1
articles.standfirst: Estado concentra 65 processos minerários ativos. Calçoene e Oiapoque lideram pesquisas associadas também ao ouro.
articles.summary: Estado concentra 65 processos minerários ativos. Calçoene e Oiapoque lideram pesquisas associadas também ao ouro.
articles.body:
O Amapá possui atualmente 65 processos minerários ativos relacionados a elementos de terras raras, todos associados a outros minerais, como o ouro. A procura por esses elementos ganhou força a partir de 2022, quando foram registrados 53 protocolos de pesquisa na Agência Nacional de Mineração (ANM).

Os municípios de Calçoene e Oiapoque concentram o maior número de protocolos de pesquisa minerária registrados no período, a maioria deles vinculada também à exploração de ouro. Essa tendência, segundo especialistas, indica que o foco das empresas está voltado principalmente para o ouro, enquanto as terras raras podem aparecer como resultado adicional das pesquisas.

Estudos realizados pelo Serviço Geológico do Brasil (SGB) apontam potencialidades de elementos de terras raras em regiões como Ferreira Gomes e Oiapoque . No entanto, ainda são necessários vultosos investimentos em pesquisa geológica para confirmar esse potencial. A possibilidade de encontrar concentrações que permitam produzir um concentrado comercialmente viável permanece incerta.

Segundo o professor Franciolli Araújo, do Instituto Federal do Amapá (Ifap) e doutor em Ciências Exatas e Tecnológicas pela Universidade Federal de Catalão, o cenário ainda é desafiador:

“Podemos ter elementos de terras raras em qualquer lugar do estado, mas em concentrações que permitam produzir um concentrado comercialmente viável, isso ainda é uma incógnita. Na minha avaliação, as empresas têm pesquisado ouro, e as terras raras poderiam ser um 'bônus' caso identifiquem em suas pesquisas”, explicou.

🔎As chamadas “terras raras” são, na verdade, um grupo de 17 elementos químicos encontrados na natureza, geralmente misturados a outros minerais, o que torna sua extração complexa e, muitas vezes, cara- daí a classificação de "raras". O Brasil detém a segunda maior reservas desses minerais, atrás apenas da China.

De acordo com o pesquisador, os investimentos podem ser feitos inicialmente pelo estado, como forma de atrair investidores, ou diretamente pelas empresas, caso existam fortes indícios da existência de depósitos. A determinação do tamanho dos depósitos e a viabilidade técnica de exploração, porém, ainda demandam muitos estudos e recursos.

A Universidade Federal de Catalão, por meio do Centro de Pesquisa em Processamento Mineral (CPMin), e o Grupo de Pesquisa em Materiais, Tecnologia, Inovação e Sustentabilidade (Matis) do Ifap, além de outras instituições, elaboraram propostas em chamadas do CNPq para coletar amostras em regiões potenciais de terras raras, inclusive no Amapá. O objetivo é caracterizar e concentrar esses minerais, etapa fundamental para confirmar a viabilidade de exploração.

Garimpo ilegal em Lourenço, Calçoene — Foto: Rafael Aleixo/Divulgaç

O Senado aprovou em 2 de setembro, o projeto que cria a Política Nacional de Minerais Críticos e Estratégicos (PNMCE). A proposta estabelece medidas para estimular a exploração e o processamento de minérios considerados estratégicos para o Brasil, incluindo a criação de um fundo garantidor e a concessão de crédito tributário de até R$ 5 bilhões.

O texto autoriza a União a participar como cotista desse fundo, com limite de R$ 2 bilhões. Apesar da participação estatal, o fundo terá natureza privada, funcionando como mecanismo de apoio a projetos e atração de investimentos para o setor mineral.

A proposta agora segue para sanção do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT).

articles.title: 260 volunteers prepared 20,000 oysters for a new reef in Britain as the Solent brings back a lost marine habitat
articles.summary: UK News: For generations, native oysters were part of life around the Solent, helping shape its coastal ecology as well as its maritime heritage. But their num.
articles.body: For generations, native oysters were part of life around the Solent, helping shape its coastal ecology as well as its maritime heritage. But their numbers have fallen dramatically, with populations declining by around 96 per cent over the past century. Now, one of Britain’s biggest marine restoration efforts is trying to bring them back. In May 2026, around 260 volunteers gathered at the University of Portsmouth to clean and prepare 20,000 native oysters before they were moved to a newly built reef in Chichester Harbour. The project marks a major step towards rebuilding one of the Solent’s most threatened marine habitats.Volunteers prepared 20,000 oysters for their return to the seaBetween 11 and 15 May, about 260 volunteers took part in a series of biosecurity days at the University of Portsmouth’s Institute of Marine Sciences. Their task was simple but important, carefully scrub, wash and inspect 20,000 native oysters before the animals were transported to their new home. The cleaning process helps remove invasive species and pathogens that could otherwise be introduced into the restoration site. Once prepared, the oysters were deployed in Chichester Harbour by the Blue Marine Foundation at the end of the week. The University said the event represented the biggest volunteer effort the initiative has seen so far.The Solent has lost most of its native oystersThe restoration comes after a dramatic collapse in the Solent’s native oyster population. According to the University of Portsmouth, numbers have declined by around 96 per cent over the past century, with overfishing, disease, invasive species and deteriorating water quality contributing to the loss. Yet oysters play an important ecological role. A single native oyster can filter up to 200 litres of water every day, while oyster reefs create shelter and habitat for hundreds of marine species. The restoration project is therefore intended to do much more than bring back an iconic shellfish, it aims to rebuild an entire underwater ecosystem.A new reef is giving the oysters somewhere to establishBefore the oysters arrived, teams created the foundation of the reef using “cultch,” a mixture of shell and stone that provides the structure needed for oysters to settle and grow. The newly cleaned animals were then placed onto this prepared habitat in Chichester Harbour, where they can begin establishing a new population. The reef forms part of the Solent Seascape Project, led by the Blue Marine Foundation with Chichester Harbour Conservancy and the University of Portsmouth. The wider initiative is working to reconnect and restore several habitats across the region, including seagrass meadows, saltmarsh, seabird nesting sites and oyster reefs.The project is bringing back a habitat that once defined the SolentOyster restoration is also an attempt to reconnect the region with its maritime past. Oyster harvesting in Chichester Harbour dates back to Roman Britain, and the shellfish once played a major role in coastal communities around the Solent. Professor Jo Preston of the University of Portsmouth said the volunteer effort was inspiring because people were helping restore a species that had once defined the area’s coastal heritage. The new reef will be monitored for five years to assess its progress. If successful, the project could demonstrate how large-scale restoration can help rebuild biodiversity while giving local communities a direct role in recovering Britain’s lost marine habitats.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘Killer bahu’: Woman danced to ‘Tum To Dhokhebaaz Ho’ as hired assailants stabbed father-in-law 26 times
articles.summary: KANPUR: A woman accused of masterminding the murder of her 63-year-old father-in-law was allegedly dancing at a lounge with her husband around the sam.
articles.body: KANPUR: A woman accused of masterminding the murder of her 63-year-old father-in-law was allegedly dancing at a lounge with her husband around the same time the killing was taking place, with police now claiming she remained in contact with the alleged assailants during the crime.A video of Shalu Minocha dancing at a lounge in Kanpur on the night her father-in-law, Vineet Minocha, was murdered surfaced on social media on Wednesday and went viral. Police said the footage, recorded by lounge staff, confirms that Shalu and her husband Subrat were at Cosmozin Lounge in Tilak Nagar that night.According to investigators, however, Shalu allegedly stayed in touch with the men she had hired to kill Vineet through WhatsApp calls, messages and voice calls and even guided them while she was at the party.The lounge's CCTV DVR was found to have no stored footage, but videos recorded by the staff showed around 20-25 people, mostly couples, dancing to Bollywood songs. Shalu was seen wearing a dark purple gown while her husband was dressed in a grey shirt.In one of the videos, the couple is seen dancing to the song Tum To Dhokhebaaz Ho, Vaada Karke Bhool Jaate Ho. Police said nothing about Shalu's behaviour appeared unusual and other guests at the lounge seemed unaware of what was allegedly unfolding at her home.Murder allegedly planned over CCTV camerasPolice arrested Shalu on Monday, alleging that she had masterminded the murder of her father-in-law after a former employee of Vineet claimed she had offered him Rs 6 lakh for the killing.Investigators suspect the alleged murder was linked to a dispute over CCTV cameras that Vineet had installed inside their apartment about 15-20 days before his death. Police said Shalu objected to the cameras, claiming they violated her privacy and caused her emotional distress.According to police, Shalu approached Vishal Gautam, a former employee at Vineet's pharmaceutical store, and allegedly gave him the original key to the family's apartment so that a duplicate could be made.Vishal then allegedly roped in his unemployed acquaintance Raj Kishor, 30, promising him an advance of Rs 30,000.Police said that on September 5, Shalu informed the accused that she, her husband and their son would be attending a party. She allegedly facilitated their entry into Ratan Orbit Apartment in Kalyanpur despite initial resistance from the security guard.The duo allegedly told the guard that they were delivering medicines, with Vishal registering himself under the fictitious name Shivam.Plan was to make murder look like heart attackAccording to investigators, Vishal and Raj hid inside a bedroom after entering the apartment using the duplicate key.Police said Shalu had allegedly instructed them to suffocate Vineet with a pillow so that his death would appear to be from a heart attack.The plan allegedly went awry when Vineet entered the bedroom around 11pm and noticed something unusual.DCP West SM Qasim Abidi said the two men panicked and allegedly attacked Vineet with knives before fleeing the apartment by jumping over the rear wall.The postmortem later revealed 26 stab wounds on Vineet's body.Police said the murder took place sometime between 10.30pm on Saturday and 3am on Sunday while Vineet was alone in the four-room apartment.Shalu and Subrat returned from the party and found Vineet's bloodied body before alerting police.Nothing stolen from houseInvestigators said CCTV footage showed Vishal and Raj leaving the apartment after the murder. They were arrested following an encounter late Sunday.After receiving medical treatment, Vishal allegedly told police that he had killed Vineet on Shalu's instructions in return for money.Police said nothing was stolen from the apartment, strengthening their suspicion that the killing was motivated by personal enmity rather than robbery. Section 61(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, relating to criminal conspiracy, has also been added to the case.Police said Shalu allegedly admitted her involvement in the presence of female police personnel after being confronted with Vishal.The investigation is continuing, with police examining the alleged communications between Shalu and the assailants as well as the circumstances surrounding the murder.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Kanpur | Silver Rate in Kanpur | Bank Holidays in Kanpur | Public Holidays in Kanpur | Kanpur AQI | Weather in Kanpur | Petrol Price in Kanpur | Diesel Price in Kanpur | CNG Price in Kanpur | LPG Price in KanpurStay updated with the latest Kanpur news. articles.title: England's mayors to be given power to introduce tourist tax
articles.summary: The government is expected to detail how local leaders will be able to impose levies on overnight stays.
articles.body:
Mayors in England are set to be given the power to introduce an overnight visitor levy on tourists, under plans being announced by the government later.

Local leaders would be allowed to bring in an uncapped levy, dubbed a "tourist tax", as a percentage of the cost of accommodation rather than a flat fee.

Hospitality leaders have warned "jobs are now at risk" because of the proposals and that families holidaying in England would feel the pinch.

But ministers are said to believe mayors are unlikely to make it too expensive with budget holidays protected by the fact it is not a flat fee.

The idea was first raised under former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer in November and is similar to schemes running in Scotland and European capitals.

The government will announce more details after the Housing Secretary Angela Rayner meets mayors in a virtual meeting held at No 10 North on Thursday.

Under the proposals, local leaders would decide how the revenue raised should be reinvested.

A government source said "it will be up to local leaders and local voters" in England "to decide what is right for their area".

But it means a holiday in England could become more expensive if local leaders decide to implement the tax.

Leading trade body UKHospitality has hit back at the proposals, warning they are "not going to be painless".

Its chief executive Allen Simpson claimed it would add about £100 to £120 on average to the cost of a family holiday in England, amid fears mayors would make use of the fact there is, in theory, no upper limit for the levy.

"We know, don't we, that local government is struggling for funds - it was hit very hard by austerity," he told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

"If you only devolve one tax raising power, of course local mayors are going to pull that lever until it snaps."

He added: "It will be the case that you'll have holiday parks which can't open in the shoulder seasons and of course people who go on holiday will just have that little bit less money in their pocket."

The Overnight Visitor Levy, which was outlined in the King's Speech in May , has not been brought forward in Parliament yet.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has framed the policy as part of his wider devolution agenda with mayors able to set out plans for how new revenues will be invested by March 2028.

He was mayor of Greater Manchester when the city introduced the City Visitor Charge in April 2023 - a £1 per room, per night fee - to pay for measures aimed at attracting more visitors.

Regional mayors say the levy is needed to raise more income to invest in local priorities and support economic growth.

The taxes are common in Europe and the rest of the world, with New York, Amsterdam and Rome applying overnight charges to accommodation stays to fund local services. However, they are capped in several European cities.

Mayor of London Sir Sadiq Khan supports a tourist tax on overnight visitors, which could raise more than £350m a year for the capital, according to analysis in January.

The figure from Central London Forward (CLF), which represents 12 central London local authorities, was based on a 3% levy on the cost of a room, whether a hotel or short-term let.

In Scotland local authorities can charge a visitor levy on overnight accommodation. In Edinburgh, the rate is 5% for those staying overnight in hotels, bed and breakfasts and self-catering facilities - capped at five nights.

In Wales, a capped levy of £1.30 per person per night is set to be introduced in April next year.

Burnham promises more devolution and public control of essential services

articles.title: Ashok Siddharth takes ‘sanyas’ from politics after Mayawati says his retirement can save Akash Anand’s future
articles.summary: LUCKNOW: Expelled BSP leader, Ashok Siddharth, on Thursday, said that he is taking 'sanyas' from politics. He is a former Rajya Sabha MP of BSP, and f.
articles.body: LUCKNOW: Expelled BSP leader, Ashok Siddharth, on Thursday, said that he is taking 'sanyas' from politics. He is a former Rajya Sabha MP of BSP, and father-in-law of BSP national president Mayawati's nephew, Akash Anand.Mayawati, on Wednesday, had said that if Ashok Siddharth retires from politics completely, it will be good for Akash Anand's political career in the party, and that he will be able to work freely in the party.On Thursday, Ashok Siddharth, in his long post on X, said, "For me, your command is the greatest. My relationships, family, everything feels utterly insignificant in front of it. Under your guidance, for the past thirty-five years, I have been devoted to the BSP and its mission . Whatever responsibilities you have entrusted to me thus far, I have strived to fulfill them with all my might. You are my political guru, my elder sister. It is because of you that I have had the privilege of serving as a member of the Legislative Council and the Rajya Sabha. You deemed someone as ordinary as me worthy enough to make a mere worker like me a part of your family. This is a debt I can never repay in this lifetime. "He also clarified that he never did anything against the interests of the party, or Mayawati. On him having an influence over Akash Anand, he added, "Let alone advising Akash Ji, I haven't even met him in the past several months except on a couple of occasions when his programs were scheduled in those states for which you had assigned me the responsibility."He also pointed out that there were people within the party who have been accusing him of trying to seize control of the party, of attempting to mislead Akash Anand, out of envy. "This is a conspiracy by my political opponents, who are themselves engaged in anti-party activities, and the truth of which will surely come before you one day or another. "He also urged Mayawati to not link his "sanyas" with Akash's return to the party, or his growth in the party. "He is your nephew before being my son-in-law. He has your blood running in his veins; he has spent two decades of his life under your shelter and care, how could an ordinary worker like me possibly mislead him? You understand his good and bad better than anyone else; whether to give him responsibility again or not is your decision," said Ashok Siddharth.He continued to request that by linking his retirement from politics to Akash Anand's career in the party, an ordinary worker like him is being given more importance than he deserves.Mayawati had recently restricted the role of Akash Anand in the party, and had allowed him to work only as an ordinary party worker. articles.title: Trump's top advisors warn him Iran war could drag through end of his term: Report
articles.summary: Middle East News: Senior White House officials have privately warned US President Donald Trump that the war with Iran could continue for the rest of his presidency, des.
articles.body: Senior White House officials have privately warned US President Donald Trump that the war with Iran could continue for the rest of his presidency, despite his public prediction that the conflict will end soon after this year’s midterm elections, The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday.Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio were among the advisers who reportedly raised the possibility during private discussions with Trump in the Oval Office and Situation Room.According to the report, the officials told Trump that Iran could continue resisting US pressure, potentially keeping the conflict going until after the next US presidential inauguration in January 2029.Trump expects 'a quick end'Trump has publicly offered a much shorter timeline for the conflict. Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, he said he expected the war to end "immediately after" the US midterm elections in November. He argued that Iran was attempting to influence the election but would not be able to maintain its resistance for much longer."I think the war will end immediately after the election... They're desperate to try and affect the election so that we could get a nice, weak group of people in there and leave them alone and let them have their nuclear weapon."Trump has also indicated that diplomatic talks remain possible, although he has said negotiations are not his preferred option.US-Iran fighting continuesTrump also referred to recent US strikes on Iran and attacks involving Iranian and American forces."We've knocked out nine of their ships; I would say that the attacks are caused by us — and you're going to see a lot more. We've taken our about nine of their tankers. Many of them are gone-zo."The US launched strikes on Iranian oil tankers during its latest offensive after Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps targeted US naval warships earlier this week.Iran has also retaliated, with multiple explosions reported over an American airbase in Jordan.Trump launched the conflict as an effort to pressure Iran over its nuclear programme. The first US strikes were carried out on February 28 as part of Operation Epic Fury, in coordination with Israel under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.The opening strikes killed Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, according to the material provided.The reported warning from Trump's senior advisers highlights the gap between the administration's private assessment of a potentially prolonged conflict and Trump's public expectation of a rapid end.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Ceuta migrant crisis: Intelligence warned of ‘mass entry’ day before 70k reached Spanish enclave
articles.summary: Europe News: Spain's intelligence and security agencies had warned of mass migration into the Spanish enclave. According to 40 documents declassified on Wednesday,.
articles.body: Spain's intelligence and security agencies had warned of mass migration into the Spanish enclave. According to 40 documents declassified on Wednesday, the government and Moroccan counterparts were warned a day before more than 70,000 people crossed into Ceuta.The documents, which include intelligence reports, alerts and internal communications from July 1 to 31, show that Spanish agencies were tracking a growing movement of migrants and online calls for a mass crossing before the surge on July 30.The disclosures have put renewed pressure on Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, who has insisted that the government had no information indicating the scale or nature of the influx that followed.Intelligence warnings came a day before surgeOn July 29, Spain's National Intelligence Centre (CNI) warned of calls on social media for migrants to enter Ceuta by climbing the border fence or swimming around it the following day.In a WhatsApp message to the Spanish government's delegation in Ceuta, the CNI warned of calls for “an assault on the fence and by sea tomorrow at 8 pm”The agency said two social media groups involved in the mobilisation had a combined 180,000 followers.“There are two different groups with a total of 180,000 followers. Just to give you an idea of the scale," the CNI wrote.The CNI also alerted Spain's Civil Guard and sent a report to Moroccan intelligence agencies DGST and DGED about plans to enter Ceuta on July 30. The warnings said migrants could try to take advantage of Morocco's annual Throne Day celebrations.A separate urgent memo referred to “several calls to carry out entries into Ceuta” on Facebook, including one group with more than 160,000 members.Warnings showed crisis was already buildingThe declassified material indicates the mass crossing did not emerge without warning.Spain's National Police border division, CENIF, said almost 1,000 people had swum into Ceuta from Morocco between July 1 and July 28. It described the increase as a “drastic upward trend compared to last year” and a “consolidated and priority threat”.A Spanish defence ministry presentation on July 30 said around 1,700 migrants had arrived by sea since July 25. It warned that “more intrusions are to be expected in the very short-term” and described the situation on the Moroccan coast near Ceuta as “migratory chaos”.The intelligence reports also said many people were already waiting to enter the water on the night of July 29. Several hundred migrants subsequently swam towards Ceuta.Documents raise questions over Morocco's roleReports issued after the crossings began also raised questions over the conduct of Moroccan security forces.A military intelligence assessment on July 30 said it was “highly likely that the Moroccan authorities are not actively encouraging the migratory wave, but have so far acted in a negligent and passive manner”.Another CNI report said: “At the operational level, no proactive response from Moroccan authorities was observed regarding the loss of control over the situation, beyond the deployment of a few riot control units.”It said the increased presence of Moroccan police and gendarmes had proved insufficient to control the crowd.The Spanish government has stopped short of saying Morocco orchestrated the episode. Sánchez said last week that there was no evidence to conclude that Moroccan authorities had planned or carried out the border rush.His position has come under renewed scrutiny after a leaked Spanish police report alleged “permissiveness” by Moroccan security forces.The Moroccan foreign ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment.Sánchez disputes warning about scaleSánchez has acknowledged that the social media campaign was known to authorities but rejected the suggestion that it amounted to a warning of the crisis that followed.“The existence of this campaign was known ... and was being monitored, but in no way did it constitute or could it be interpreted as an indicator of the scale, nature, or probability of what happened afterward,” Sánchez wrote on X on Wednesday.Foreign Minister Jose Manuel Albares also defended the government's position.“I am speaking as Spain's foreign minister, within my remit and based on what I experienced that day. I was not aware of any information of any kind pointing to the magnitude of the avalanche,” Albares told reporters.The government argues that while agencies knew about planned crossings, the intelligence did not indicate that tens of thousands of migrants would enter Ceuta.Crisis continues weeks after mass crossingThe July 30-31 surge has also left a prolonged humanitarian crisis in the Spanish enclave.NGOs estimate that more than 140 migrants died during the mass crossing. Local authorities say more than 10,000 migrants, including unaccompanied minors, remain in Ceuta, while the national government has put the figure at around 5,000.Many are living in makeshift camps or on streets and beaches. The situation has triggered near-daily protests by residents angry over the government's handling of the crisis.The release of the documents is expected to intensify the political dispute over whether Spanish authorities acted quickly enough despite receiving warnings in the days and hours before the mass crossing.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Spanish cave remains reveal repeated cannibalism in prehistoric Europe, from violent deaths to human skulls turned into cups
articles.summary: Europe News: Ancient human remains from three caves in southern Spain are revealing a disturbing but complex chapter in Europe’s prehistoric past. Researchers exam.
articles.body: Ancient human remains from three caves in southern Spain are revealing a disturbing but complex chapter in Europe’s prehistoric past. Researchers examined nearly 1,000 human bones from Malalmuerzo, Carigüela and Majolicas caves in Granada, finding evidence that people cut, fractured, chewed and deliberately modified human remains during different periods of the Neolithic. The findings suggest cannibalism was not one continuous tradition, but a practice that appeared repeatedly in different contexts over thousands of years, offering clues about prehistoric violence, death and ritual.Ancient Spanish caves preserve evidence of repeated cannibalismThe remains come from three caves in Granada that have provided archaeologists with evidence of prehistoric human activity for decades. Researchers in 'Multiphase human cannibalism in Neolithic southern Iberia: Chronological and taphonomic evidence from Malalmuerzo, Carigüela, and Majolicas Caves,' published in Journal of Archaeological Science examined the bones for microscopic traces including cut marks, fractures, impact damage and tooth marks, while also studying how and when the damage occurred. Their analysis found evidence consistent with deliberate processing of human remains at all three sites, although the circumstances varied considerably. At Malalmuerzo, some remains appear connected with violent deaths, while Carigüela contained deliberately modified human skulls. At Majolicas, the treatment of human remains appears to have had a different cultural context, showing that the discovery cannot be reduced to one explanation for prehistoric cannibalism.Cannibalism appeared during several distinct prehistoric periodsRather than suggesting that Neolithic Europeans regularly consumed human flesh, the evidence indicates several separate episodes spread across thousands of years. The researchers identified concentrations around the end of the sixth millennium BC, the middle of the fifth millennium BC and the end of the third millennium BC. At Carigüela, evidence indicates several episodes of cannibalism during the Neolithic, including the deliberate modification of two human skulls into cup-like objects. At Majolicas, the most recent evidence dates to approximately 3800 BC. The pattern suggests that cannibalism repeatedly emerged under particular circumstances rather than representing a permanent or universal feature of prehistoric communities.Some remains reveal possible episodes of prehistoric violenceOne of the most striking sets of evidence comes from Malalmuerzo, where fractures and other damage to the bones indicate that some individuals may have died violently. The remains belonged to people of different ages, leading researchers to consider whether a group could have been attacked, killed and subsequently consumed. This interpretation potentially connects cannibalism with conflict between prehistoric communities. However, the researchers do not treat every damaged bone as proof of warfare. The contrasting evidence from the three caves demonstrates that human remains could be processed in different ways and for different reasons, including possible conflict, consumption and cultural or ritual practices.Human skulls were transformed into objects after deathThe discoveries at Carigüela offer some of the clearest evidence that the treatment of human remains was not necessarily motivated by hunger alone. Two skulls were deliberately modified into cups, suggesting that parts of the human body could acquire a new symbolic or practical purpose after death. The researchers therefore argue against viewing “Neolithic cannibalism” as one uniform practice. Similar marks on human bones can emerge from very different circumstances, and the archaeological record points towards a complicated relationship between death, the body and community life. These recurring episodes provide a rare glimpse into how prehistoric societies dealt with violence, the dead and relationships between groups.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: How Delhi bomber planned to make explosives from ‘urine’
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Umar-un-Nabi, accused in the 2025 Red Fort car blast, stored his urine in a polythene bag while hiding in Nuh, according to the NIA charges.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Umar-un-Nabi, accused in the 2025 Red Fort car blast, stored his urine in a polythene bag while hiding in Nuh, according to the NIA chargesheet.The unusual practice came to light after the woman who owned the house complained to her husband about a foul smell from the room.According to the agency, he did not leave the room to dispose of his urine and instead stored it in a polythene bag.“He did not go outside to dispose of it and thus a foul smell was emanating from the room, prompting the woman to complain to her husband,” the chargesheet said.According to NIA, a PDF recovered from the pen drives of the accused described a method for preparing explosive substances using 'urea nitrate' and referred to an alternative source of urea.“Interestingly, an innovative method for preparing explosive substances using urea nitrate has been elaborated in a PDF material seized from the pen drives of the accused wherein an alternative method for the source of urea is mentioned as — ‘extracting urea from urine’.”The NIA has alleged that Nabi, who was killed in the November 2025 Red Fort car blast, was the mastermind and operational in-charge of a revived Ansar Ghazwat-ul-Hind (AGuH) terror module.According to the chargesheet, Nabi, also known as Pinda and Rahul Bhat, had been working since early 2022 to revive the dormant module and build a network of radicalised people for carrying out terrorist activities.The agency described him as the “operational in-charge” of AGuH Interim, which it identified as a revived manifestation of Al-Qaida.The NIA has alleged that Nabi radicalised recruits, glorified acts of “Shahadat” or martyrdom, arranged clandestine meetings, facilitated terror training and managed logistics for the module.The chargesheet also says he had planned to travel to Afghanistan for “Hijrat” as his association with the group’s extremist ideology grew.'Lone Mujahid Pocket Book'The agency has also referred to the seizure of a terror manual, “Lone Mujahid Pocket Book”, which was published in “Inspire” magazine, affiliated with Al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP), and was allegedly being followed by the module.According to the NIA, the manual contained operational information relating to explosives, weapons, vehicles, arson and covert activities, including chapters on TATP and remote-control mechanisms for detonating IEDs.The chargesheet says Nabi also bought a new T-shirt, a wine-coloured shirt and green-coloured cargo pants from a shop in Nuh on November 7, paying in cash.A revived moduleThe NIA alleges that Nabi and other members of the module possessed and circulated extremist literature advocating armed struggle and violence.The material examined during the investigation included documents titled “Definition of Jihad”, “The Requirements of Jihad”, “The 21 Aims and Objectives of Jihad”, “39 Ways to Serve and Participate in Jihad” and “44 Ways to Support Jihad”.According to the agency, the literature sought to justify violent extremism and portrayed armed struggle as a religious obligation.The material also allegedly contained instructions on operational secrecy, concealment, the use of false identities and different forms of terrorist attacks.The accused allegedly remained in contact through encrypted messaging applications, including Signal.The NIA has further alleged that Nabi helped arrange funds, procure illegal weapons and secure locations for members of the module and materials linked to the alleged conspiracy.Meetings were allegedly held in Jammu and Kashmir and Delhi-NCR, where members were trained and preparations made for terrorist activities.The Red Fort blastThe agency says the vehicle that exploded near the Red Fort on November 10, 2025 had been converted into a vehicle-borne improvised explosive device (VBIED).According to the chargesheet, Nabi and a co-accused had procured a second-hand car as part of the alleged conspiracy.Nabi was inside the vehicle when it exploded, the chargesheet states. DNA examination of biological material recovered from the blast site allegedly confirmed his identity.Forensic examination of post-blast material detected traces of TATP and ammonium nitrate, according to the NIA.The agency has alleged that the explosive device was initiated from inside the vehicle through a command mechanism.The blast took place at around 6.50pm near the Red Fort. Eleven people were killed and 29 injured, according to the investigation. The explosion also damaged surrounding property and vehicles.The NIA has alleged that the attack was the culmination of a wider conspiracy involving the revival of the AGuH module, radicalisation of recruits and preparations for terrorist activities.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: Russia outpacing Ukraine's air defences with daily use of new jet-powered drones
articles.summary: The new models can travel at speeds of up to 300mph, faster than Ukraine's air defence interceptors.
articles.body:
Russia fired its new rapid, jet-powered drones against Ukraine every day throughout August, BBC Verify analysis of Ukrainian Air Force data has found, escalating its use of a weapon that Kyiv's air defences are struggling to deal with.

It marked the first time that daily attacks by Moscow's new upgraded Geran drones were recorded in Ukrainian Air Force data. The growing use of jet-propelled and other varieties of drones prompted President Volodymyr Zelensky to condemn what he called an unfolding "horror" over the skies of Kyiv.

Ukraine's military recently told the BBC that jet-powered drone attacks grew from 350 in June to 1,600 in July and 2,800 in August. In five of the nightly attacks in August, these drones outnumbered the older, slower models.

"The reason for turning to jet-powered drones is that they are much faster than the previous generation and it makes it much more difficult for Ukraine to intercept them," said Dr Marina Miron, an expert on military technology at King's College London.

The upgraded munitions can cruise at more than 300mph, significantly faster than older models and well beyond the top speed of Kyiv's interceptors. The drones are powered by turbojet engines, some of which, according to Ukrainian military intelligence, are sourced from China.

According to Zelensky, the drones were used as part of a wave of attacks that killed at least 12 people and injured 20 more on 1 September. Six of the casualties were railway workers after a depot was hit in Kyiv.

Earlier this year Ukraine showed relative success in countering Russian drones and was intercepting 94% of long-range drones, according to Zelensky . But the speed of the newer drones has prompted the latest round in Kyiv and Moscow's arms race. On 10 August, Ukraine's deputy head of military intelligence, Maj Gen Vadym Skibitskyi, said his forces needed new interceptor missiles "capable of matching [jet-drones'] speed".

Four Ukrainian companies have reportedly started testing missiles that can shoot down the new Geran models, officials in Kyiv recently told reporters. The country's new defence minister, Yevhenii Khmara, has tasked them with producing "thousands of units" as quickly as possible.

Russia also had an economic incentive to invest in the jet-powered drones. The increased speed and manoeuvrability of these models means the line between them and more expensive cruise missiles has become "blurred", said John Hardie of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a think tank focused on national security and foreign policy.

"Long-range one-way attack drones are basically a poor man's cruise missile," he said. "The more you add capability to a drone, the less meaningful the distinction between the drone and a lower-end cruise missile."

But the analyst organisation Conflict Armament Research emphasised that jet-drones are not yet as advanced as cruise missiles. It said the munitions have a shorter attack range, carry much smaller warheads and are more susceptible to jamming systems.

Meanwhile, satellite images appear to show Moscow is redesigning key facilities dedicated to fighting the war in Ukraine to host jet-powered drones, with longer rails associated with the munitions visible at an entirely new base at Tsymbulova in the Oryol region.

Multiple launch sites appear to have been built at the facility, which is around 109 miles (175 km) from the Ukrainian border.

Since the facility became operational, Tsymbulova appears to have become a key centre for Russian drone attacks. Oryol region, where the Tsymbulova base is located, was not mentioned as a drone launch site in Air Force reports before September 2024, but by August 2026 it was named in almost every attack.

The proliferation of jet-powered drones comes as BBC Verify found that Russia is now striking Ukraine with complex attacks involving hundreds of drones and missiles about once a week.

The increase in the size of the strikes is being powered by Moscow's shift towards combining a "greater variety of munitions" - including jet-powered and decoy drones - with expensive ballistic missiles that are extremely difficult to intercept, analyst Michael Bohnert of the RAND think tank told BBC Verify. Kyiv's data shows that Moscow is now using over 15 times more drones per attack than it was four years ago.

Bohnert added that the tactically complicated nature of the assaults, coupled with a global shortage of air defence systems capable of halting ballistic missiles partly caused by the US-Israeli war with Iran, has led to falling interception rates by Ukraine.

Ukraine's Air Force data showed a drop in interceptions of ballistic missiles up to the end of July. In August, Kyiv mostly stopped publishing the figures that would show its interception rate.

articles.title: Elon Musk’s estranged daughter takes aim at father and AI in a new fashion campaign: “He was designed to obey. Not me.”
articles.summary: US News: Elon Musk’s estranged daughter Vivian Wilson has taken aim at artificial intelligence in a new fashion campaign. The 22-year-old is the face of Spanis.
articles.body: Elon Musk’s estranged daughter Vivian Wilson has taken aim at artificial intelligence in a new fashion campaign. The 22-year-old is the face of Spanish fashion brand Desigual’s Fall 2026 campaign, “Born to Disobey”, in which she takes control of a malfunctioning humanoid robot and mocks its inability to understand human behaviour.The campaign is drawing particular attention because Wilson’s father is Elon Musk, the billionaire behind Tesla, SpaceX and xAI and one of the most prominent promoters of AI. Vivian does not name Musk in the campaign, but its anti-AI message and references to obedience have prompted attention because of Wilson’s publicly strained relationship with her father.In the campaign film, Wilson is shown with a robot called DESI84. She uses it as a golf tee, walks it on a leash and tries to teach it to say “Desigual”. The robot repeatedly malfunctions, while Wilson remains in control of the situation. One of the campaign's lines says, “He was designed to obey. Not me.” The film ends with Wilson saying: “Some things aren’t meant to be fixed.”A robot that ‘was designed to obey’The campaign contains several lines that have attracted attention because of Wilson’s relationship with Musk. One of them says: “He was designed to obey. Not me.” The robot has also been compared by various media with Tesla’s Optimus humanoid robot, although neither Wilson nor Desigual has said that DESI84 represents Musk or Tesla. The symbolism is nevertheless hard to miss. Wilson, whose father is one of the world's best-known technology billionaires, is now fronting a campaign that questions the growing role of AI and celebrates human imperfection instead.Wilson says AI threatens creative jobsWilson has been direct about why she agreed to front the campaign. Speaking to People, she said she was concerned about AI’s impact on the fashion industry because it can take jobs away from creative professionals and also has environmental consequences.“Art is emotion through expression,” Wilson said. “Since emotion is inherently human, AI takes away any underlying intention and replaces it with plagiarized colors and shapes.”Wilson and Musk have a strained relationshipThe campaign comes against the backdrop of Wilson’s long-running public estrangement from Musk. She is the daughter of Musk and Canadian author Justine Wilson. Her parents married in 2000 and divorced in 2008. They had six children together, including Wilson’s twin brother and younger triplets. As per various media reports,Vivian began her gender transition at 16 with the consent of both parents. Musk later claimed that he had been “tricked into signing documents” related to her transition. Wilson has disputed his version of events and said her father was aware of what was happening.In 2022, at 18, she legally changed her name from Xavier Alexander Musk to Vivian Jenna Wilson, taking her mother’s surname and asking the court to remove Musk from her name.In the court filing, Wilson said she no longer wished to be related to her biological father “in any way, shape or form”. She has since publicly distanced herself from Musk.Elon has also spoken publicly about their relationship. He has referred to his child as “dead” and blamed what he called the “woke mind virus” for their estrangement. Vivian, in turn, has criticised her father publicly, including on social media. She has previously spoken about his role in her childhood and their relationship.Why the campaign is drawing attentionThe campaign does not directly identify Musk as its target. But with Wilson publicly estranged from one of the world's most influential technology figures, her decision to front an advertisement questioning AI has inevitably brought their relationship back into focus.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Buy now or wait and hope? Families face gamble on heating oil
articles.summary: The price of heating oil has almost doubled in 12 months following the conflict in the Middle East.
articles.body:
As the summer draws to a close, families who rely on fuel oil to heat their homes are facing a dilemma.

The price has almost doubled over the past year, following the outbreak of conflict between the US and Iran.

It has left people wondering whether to buy now for the winter, or hold off in the hope that prices will fall – with the risk that they could rise again.

John Craggs, 73, from Wigtoft, near Boston, Lincolnshire, needs to fill his tank ahead of winter.

"Over the next few weeks I'll be monitoring the price to see if it goes down a little bit and then order the oil," he says.

But whatever they decide, he and his wife Libby, 80, are planning to limit their heating this winter because of the cost.

"We've both had health problems over the last few years and we should be keeping warm but its just too expensive," John Craggs adds.

"We will only have the heating on up to about 17 degrees in three of the rooms in the house, between about 3pm and 8pm, just to keep the cost down to be able to afford it."

About 1.5 million UK households use heating oil, typically in rural areas. This includes more than 40% of homes in some parts of Lincolnshire, including Wainfleet All Saints, Wragby, Roughton and Ludford, according to Census data.

Unlike gas and electricity customers, they are not covered by the energy price cap, leaving them more exposed to sudden increases. They also have to pay a lump sum in advance for their fuel, with domestic tanks typically holding between 1,000 and 2,000 litres.

On Wednesday, the average price was 97.05p per litre, according to the comparison website boilerjuice.com , which measures the cost for purchases of 1,000 litres.

That figure is up by 85% since 9 September 2025, when it stood at 52.8p, and while it has dropped significantly from a high of 134p in March, prices have been climbing again in recent weeks after renewed fighting between the US and Iran .

It means a household wanting to fill a 1,000-litre tank could be facing a bill of more than £970.

In March, the government announced a support package worth £53m for low-income families who use heating oil after prices surged due to the conflict in the Middle East.

The funding is distributed by local authorities, which set their own criteria for eligibility.

John Craggs says he inquired about help, but found he did not qualify.

The charity National Energy Action wants to see the price cap that covers gas and electricity extended to include all forms of energy, including heating oil.

It is also calling on the government to provide more help to households.

Matt Copeland, the group's interim director of policy, said: "I don't think the level of support really anticipated the length of time these high prices would go on for. It's really important that the government does look at that again in the budget and allocates more funding to help people to afford their heating.

"The government should also look at widening the criteria so the low-income households outside of the benefit system who are really struggling to afford their energy bills can access the support that they need."

A spokesperson for the Department of Energy Security and Net Zero said: "Energy is an everyday essential and needs to be affordable for everyone, which is why we have cut VAT on electricity bills to give families breathing space.

"This follows taking £150 in costs off bills earlier this year, and we will keep looking at what more we can do to protect households."

articles.title: 'I use Zumba to better the lives of my community in Gorleston'
articles.summary: Berna Akinal says the fitness-dance class can be a "release" from the difficulties in life.
articles.body:
Growing up in Istanbul, Zumba instructor Berna Akinal said for as long as she could remember she has always wanted to dance.

After moving to Norwich in 1984, she spent 25 years working as an accountant before she lost her job and took up the dance-fitness workout as a hobby.

In 2012 Akinal obtained her licence to teach classes and later set up Team Berna Zumba Club in Gorleston-on-Sea, Norfolk, which now has 200 members and runs four classes a week.

Akinal, who has been nominated for BBC Norfolk Make a Difference Award, said: "I use [Zumba] to better the lives of people in my community - I don't have children so the people who come to my classes are my family."

Akinal moved to the UK to study at the University of East Anglia in Norwich, before she met and married her English husband 32 years ago.

She said the pair had been pen friends before she had moved from Turkey.

"I wanted to learn English from the age of two. My dad, who was a dentist, loved British music, film and artists so I grew up with all of that in the house.

"He bought me BBC tapes so I could learn to speak BBC English - so when I arrived here I was speaking like that," said Akinal.

"My dad is 91 now, but he gave me my passion for music and dancing.

"When I first started Zumba I thought only a few people would turn up, maybe my mum and a faithful friend. I never thought in a million years it would grow into this big happy family, " she added.

Akinal added that the classes made the biggest difference to her attendees during the Covid lockdowns.

"All the online classes were free. It kept everybody fit and it kept my mind fit, because we all went through dark times - watching the news and losing loved ones," she said.

Akinal added that she has experienced health issues while teaching Zumba, which have often made her feel tired, and has been supporting family members through cancer treatment.

"Whatever is going on in the world - wars, illnesses, floods - the moment we step in here it's our happy place with a magical atmosphere.

"Just for an hour we can dance and be happy and all be Beyoncé or Shakira - just don't look in the mirror! We just get a lift and with music we can travel the world," she said.

"I think 90% of my success is down to my mum Necla. She's our Zumba Queen - our Zumba mummy. She makes everyone welcome as soon as they walk in. She's 82 and she's so hip and cool, " Akinal added.

Team Berna is nominated in the Active category at the BBC Norfolk Make a Difference Awards, which will be held on Thursday at St Andrew's Hall in Norwich.

The group was nominated by Dawn Sandell, one of Akinal's class members who has been involved with the group for 10 years.

Sandell said: "Berna and her mum do so much for the community, raising charity money, seeing people outside of Zumba for a chat or lunch.

"She makes us all feel like family. If we don't go for a week she always checks we are OK, and she remembers things in our lives and really cares."

articles.title: In 1981, Australia built its first solar power station at remote White Cliffs; 14 dishes powered a hospital, school, post office and 12 homes, and 45 years later the site is heritage listed
articles.summary: Rest of World News: On the edge of the outback in far western New South Wales, a cluster of silver dishes once turned toward the sun, capturing light in a place where the.
articles.body: On the edge of the outback in far western New South Wales, a cluster of silver dishes once turned toward the sun, capturing light in a place where the grid had never reached. In 1981, Australia’s first solar power station began operating at remote White Cliffs, using 14 parabolic dishes to generate electricity for a small community that included a hospital, school, post office and 12 homes. For more than a decade, the plant proved that solar energy could reliably power a town in one of the harshest environments on the continent. Now, 45 years after it first switched on, the site has been formally recognised as part of the state’s heritage, a quiet landmark that marks the beginning of Australia’s journey into large scale solar power.As reported by the NSW Office of Environment and Heritage and ABC News, the listing ensures that the story of White Cliffs will be preserved alongside the physical remnants of the pioneering plant.A town beyond the end of the gridWhite Cliffs is a tiny settlement in the semi arid plains of north western New South Wales, not far from the South Australian border. In the late 20th century, it was home to a few dozen people, many of them workers and their families associated with local mining and pastoral activities. Like many remote Australian communities, it sat far beyond the reach of the main electricity network. Running diesel generators was expensive, logistically challenging and environmentally costly, with fuel needing to be trucked in over long distances.In this context, solar power was an appealing alternative. The region enjoys plenty of sunshine for most of the year, with clear skies and high solar irradiance. If a system could be designed to reliably capture and convert that energy, it could reduce dependence on diesel and provide a more sustainable power source for critical services.The birth of a solar experimentThe White Cliffs solar power station was envisaged as a demonstration project, a real world test of whether solar thermal technology could meet the needs of a remote community. Completed in 1981, the plant consisted of 14 parabolic dish collectors, each mounted on a tracking system that followed the sun across the sky. The dishes concentrated sunlight onto receivers that heated a working fluid, which in turn drove a generator to produce electricity. The system was connected to the local mini grid, supplying power to critical community infrastructure.The hospital, school and post office relied on the solar station for much of their electricity, as did 12 residential homes. Batteries stored energy for use when the sun was not shining, and diesel generators remained in place as backup for extended cloudy periods or maintenance.For the time, the project was technologically ambitious. Solar power was still a niche field, and large scale applications were rare anywhere in the world. White Cliffs became a reference point for engineers, policymakers and researchers interested in the potential of renewable energy in remote areas.Proving that solar could work in the outbackThe White Cliffs station proved that solar energy was far more than a lab experiment. It provided reliable power to a remote outback town, while enduring choking dust, blistering heat and wild temperature swings. Running it was hard work. Crews had to constantly clean dirty mirrors, and fix complicated tracking equipment in a small town without specialized mechanics. Primitive battery technology also proved a constant challenge to store power for the nite. Yet the plant ran successfully for more than a decade, drawing international attention and local pride.But the station closed by the mid-1990s due to changing energy policies and newer technology. The dishes stopped turning and the site fell silent, a monument in waiting to early solar pioneering work. As enormous solar farms started to proliferate across Australia, an interest in its history grew. In 2026, the New South Wales government formally added the White Cliffs plant to the state heritage register. The move protects the remaining structures and pays tribute to the trailblazing project that showed off-grid clean energy actually could work.What the heritage listing meansThe heritage status does not aim to return the plant to full operation, but to preserve its significance as a landmark in energy history.Interpretive signage, conservation of key structures and careful management of the site will allow visitors and researchers to understand what once took place there. For local residents, the listing is a recognition of their town’s place in a broader national story, one that is increasingly relevant as Australia expands its solar and renewable capacity.For the wider public, White Cliffs offers a tangible connection to the early days of solar power. It is easy to think of renewable energy as a recent phenomenon, driven by 21st century climate concerns and technological advances. The White Cliffs station reminds us that serious investment in solar began decades ago, in places where the economic and logistical case was clearest. The dishes that once turned toward the sun were not just machines. They were a statement that remote communities did not have to rely solely on diesel and that the outback’s sunlight could be turned into a local asset.A quiet pioneer in a solar futureToday, Australia is home to some of the world’s largest solar farms and highest rates of rooftop photovoltaic installation.The technology has changed, with photovoltaic panels now more common than parabolic dishes for many applications. Yet the basic idea remains the same: capture abundant sunlight and convert it into electricity for homes, businesses and public services.White Cliffs sits at the beginning of that arc. It was a small, remote experiment, but it helped build confidence in solar power at a time when the technology was still unproven at scale. The heritage listing ensures that this chapter will not be forgotten as newer, larger projects come online.Visitors who travel to the site now will find a landscape marked by both absence and presence. The dishes may no longer move, but their bases and supporting structures remain. The control buildings and substations still stand, weathered but intact. Information panels tell the story of how, in 1981, a handful of solar collectors powered a hospital, school, post office and homes in a town far from the grid. In that story lies the outline of a future that Australia is still building, one in which the sun plays a central role in powering communities from the coast to the outback.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
