articles.body: The latest Congress-National Conference (NC) clash may have begun with a song, but it is really about something much older: who gets to set the political terms of the alliance in Jammu and Kashmir?CM Omar Abdullah and NC president Farooq Abdullah stood through the full rendition of Vande Mataram on Wednesday at the inaugural International Film Festival in Srinagar. The song was played in its complete six-stanza version, lasting about three minutes and 10 seconds, in line with the Centre's new protocol.This was in sharp contrast with the Congress's stand. Its grand-old party has reaffirmed its 1937 decision to restrict public rendition at party events to the first two stanzas, arguing that the later verses sit uneasily with the pluralist ethos of the freedom movement.Congress general secretary KC Venugopal subsequently said the full version "sits uneasily" with the syncretic and pluralist ethos envisioned by India's freedom fighters and urged allies to stand by the Congress position.The NC was quick to respond, saying the J&K government was only fulfilling its official duty. "After legislative enactment by Parliament, singing Vande Mataram and standing for the song has become a statutory obligation (mandatory legal duty) regardless of the ideological position of any party, group or alliance," said National Conference spokesperson Tanvir Sadiq.The Vande Mataram row is the latest in the list of NC-Congress differences that have surfaced post-election. However, in J&K, the dispute carries an additional historical charge.The NC has spent decades constructing its political identity around a particular proposition: New Delhi can be a partner, but it cannot be the political proprietor of Kashmir's choices.That is where the ghost of 1987 enters.One alliance, two political vocabulariesThe Vande Mataram dispute has once again exposed an asymmetry that has repeatedly surfaced between the two parties.Congress has to balance its position across India. For Abdullahs' NC, the principal political constituency remains rooted in J&K, where questions of identity, autonomy, federalism and the relationship with New Delhi carry a much more immediate electoral meaning.It is also why the latest row is not an isolated irritant in the alliance.In December 2025, for instance, Omar Abdullah explicitly distanced the NC from Congress's "vote chori" campaign, saying Congress was free to choose its own agenda but that it was not automatically the agenda of the INDIA bloc. With this, Omar tried to assert his party's political autonomy within the alliance.And that has been the recurring pattern.The alliance and an unequal power equationThe 2024 assembly election gave the NC-Congress relationship a new lease of life, but it also made the asymmetry between the two parties stark.The alliance crossed the majority mark with 49 seats, with the NC winning 42, Congress six and CPM one. The BJP emerged with 29, PDP three and independents seven.The pre-poll negotiations themselves had not been effortless: the parties agreed that NC would contest 51 seats and Congress 32, while several constituencies remained "friendly contests".The campaign also revealed the limits of joint ownership. Congress and NC leaders did not always campaign together. In Sopore, where the two allies were in a friendly contest, Rahul Gandhi and Omar Abdullah campaigned for their respective candidates separately.(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(`message`,function(e){if(e.data[`datawrapper-height`]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(`iframe`);for(var n in e.data[`datawrapper-height`])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[`datawrapper-height`][n]+`px`;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();During the campaign, Omar Abdullah had publicly noted that Rahul Gandhi should dedicate more campaign time and effort to the Jammu region in addition to Kashmir to maximise electoral impact.Omar himself gave the practical reason for the alliance during the campaign: it was intended to prevent a hung assembly and give voters an alternative.The alliance won the election, and the next question was: what does each side get to claim as its own?The first major post-election rupture came even before the new government had settled in.Omar Abdullah became CM in October 2024, but Congress chose to stay out of his ministry, citing restoration of statehood as its priority. While Congress backed the NC government from outside, its absence highlighted a strategic divide within the alliance. Omar had to engage with Delhi to govern the Union Territory, while Congress sought to pressure the Centre from outside. That difference in approach has repeatedly resurfaced.Statehood: Common demand & source of frictionIn July 2025, Congress announced protests in Jammu, Srinagar and Delhi and Rahul Gandhi and Mallikarjun Kharge wrote to PM Narendra Modi seeking legislation to restore J&K's statehood. The NC leadership was irritated because the announcement had not been coordinated with the ruling party. Some NC leaders described Congress's campaign as counterproductive and even as "sabotage" of the government's own efforts.Omar's objection was that Congress had launched the campaign without informing or consulting the NC, leaving its alliance partner caught off guard.The difference is clearer on Article 370. The NC's 2024 manifesto explicitly called for the restoration of Articles 370 and 35A and reversal of the changes made after August 2019. Congress has similarly opposed the 2019 constitutional changes, but in its recent campaigns placed greater emphasis on the restoration of statehood.Omar reiterated in the J&K assembly in February that his government remained committed to restoring special status, even as statehood remained an immediate demand. By July 2026, he was also linking the restoration of statehood to any future discussion on J&K's earlier constitutional position.This has given the two parties different political priorities.The Rajya Sabha disputeIn October 2025, the disagreement moved from ideology to seats. J&K was electing four Rajya Sabha members. The NC, which had emerged as the dominant party in the assembly, initially discussed leaving one seat for Congress.Talks failed.The NC eventually fielded candidates for all four seats after Congress decided not to contest the fourth seat it had been offered, arguing that it was not among the "safe seats" it had sought.Omar's response was strikingly matter-of-fact: "So be it."The NC-Congress disagreement ultimately cost the alliance a clean sweep, with the BJP winning the fourth seat Congress had declined to contest.We felt that the best chance of winning that seat was with the Congress, and they felt otherwise. So be it.The ghost of 1987To understand why the NC may be particularly sensitive to questions of control, one has to go back not merely to 1987 but to 1984.Farooq Abdullah's government was dismissed on July 2, 1984, after 12 NC legislators defected. Ghulam Mohammad Shah, Farooq's brother-in-law and leader of the defecting group, formed the government with Congress support. Contemporary accounts described the episode as a central-government intervention in Kashmir politics; Farooq called the dismissal unconstitutional.For the NC, this was not an abstract constitutional episode. It was a direct lesson in the vulnerability of a regional government to New Delhi's political machinery.Then came 1986.Rajiv Gandhi and Farooq Abdullah reached an agreement that brought the two parties together electorally. A Human Rights Watch report noted that the accord deepened a sense of betrayal among many Kashmiris, who saw Farooq Abdullah compromising with the same Congress party that had pushed him out of office two years earlier.1987: The alliance that became a warningThe NC-Congress alliance won 66 of J&K's 76 assembly seats in 1987. But the result was overshadowed by the emergence of the Muslim United Front as an opposition platform, arrests of its candidates and workers, and widespread allegations of electoral rigging. Human Rights Watch later described the election as a turning point that contributed to widespread disillusionment with electoral politics.The significance of 1987 for the NC, therefore, is about the political memory it created. A generation of Kashmiri activists came to believe that the democratic route had been closed to them, a perception that became part of the backdrop to the insurgency that followed.The episode also left an enduring paradox. Congress was simultaneously the NC's electoral partner and a major force at the Centre. That history helps explain the NC's instinct to work with Congress while resisting any perception that Delhi is dictating its regional agenda.That distrust predates the 1980s. In 1953, Sheikh Abdullah was dismissed and arrested after his relationship with the Union government deteriorated. The circumstances were very different, but the political memory was similar: central intervention could reshape J&K's politics. For the NC, unlike many other regional parties, Congress's centralising past is therefore not distant history but part of its own political inheritance.2009-14: History managed, but not erasedThe two parties showed they could overcome that history after the 2008 assembly election. The NC won 28 seats and Congress 17, and the parties formed a coalition government with Omar Abdullah as CM in 2009.But the partnership remained contested. Differences over AFSPA, administrative issues and governance repeatedly surfaced. In 2011, Congress called for consensus on AFSPA while Omar maintained that the state government was an important stakeholder.By 2014, the alliance had run its course and Congress chose to contest the assembly election separately. NC leaders argued that the association with a centrist national party had diluted the party's pro-Valley credentials, with one senior NC leader calling Congress a "very bad alliance partner".The 1987 ghost & real test of allianceWhile 1987 may still shape the NC's political instincts, it would be too simplistic to link every present-day disagreement to that history. The political and constitutional context has changed; however, the experience remains part of the backdrop to the relationship.The lesson for the NC, as we saw in the last election, has not been to avoid Congress, but to work with it where interests converge while retaining its own political space.The Vande Mataram dispute, therefore, is less significant in itself than what it reveals about continuing differences over statehood, Article 370, seat-sharing and the balance between Congress's national strategy and the NC's regional politics.The alliance can survive such differences, but the interesting question now is how durable it will be, which willdepend on how well the two parties manage their competing political priorities.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Get off our roads Mr Singh': Trump administration's 'self-deport' advertisement sparks row
articles.summary: US News: A US department of homeland security (DHS) social media post targeting Indian Americans with the warning “self-deport or find out” has sparked an onli.
articles.body: A US department of homeland security (DHS) social media post targeting Indian Americans with the warning “self-deport or find out” has sparked an online backlash, with critics calling the campaign “racist” and “anti-Indian”.The AI-generated post, shared by the official DHS account on X amid the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown, uses characters from the Transformers franchise.It features Optimus Prime, the franchise’s protagonist, confronting a brown-bearded man, “Mr Singh” with the message: “Self-deport or find out”.The post also carries the message: “Get off our roads, you don’t know how to drive Mr Singh”, drawing further criticism over its reference to the common Indian and Sikh surname.The campaign is part of the administration’s broader crackdown on illegal immigration and immigrant truck drivers.A related video features Megatron, the franchise’s antagonist, seeking the release of truck drivers Harjinder Singh, Rajinder Kumar, Bekzhan Beishekeev, Akhror Bozorov and Jasveer Singh, who were involved in road accidents and other crimes.“If you approach this nation with hostile intent, know this. We will defend ourselves. We will defend Americanism. We will defend our home,” the DHS said in an X post.The use of “Mr Singh” in the campaign drew sharp criticism from advocacy groups, including the Hindu American Foundation (HAF) and Sikh Coalition.“‘Singhs’ are Hindu, they are Sikhs, they are American and they drive. Racist, un-American, anti-Indian profiling/trolling by @DHSgov should shock our nation’s collective conscience,” HAF said in a post on X.“This is a discriminatory post by a federal agency that is far beyond political messaging, and we welcome an investigation,” the foundation said, tagging Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K Dhillon and FBI Director Kash Patel.The Sikh Coalition also criticised the campaign, saying Sikhs continue to face profiling based on their appearance.“Twenty-five years after 9/11, Sikhs are still being targeted and profiled for how we look,” the organisation said, news agency PTI reported.“Millions of Sikhs in the United States have the last name Singh, which means lion. We remain fearless in identifying as Sikhs – even when our government portrays us as enemies,” it added.The controversy comes as the DHS promotes its CBP Home programme, which allows eligible undocumented migrants to register their intention to voluntarily leave the United States.Migrants who register for self-deportation can receive travel assistance and an exit bonus of $2,600, according to the DHS.The campaign's focus on commercial drivers comes amid a broader US crackdown on undocumented migrants working in the trucking industry.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: UP horror: 7-month-pregnant woman beaten to death by husband in Hardoi
articles.summary: LUCKNOW: A 24-year-old woman, who was around seven months pregnant, was allegedly beaten to death with a wooden stick by her husband following a domes.
articles.body: LUCKNOW: A 24-year-old woman, who was around seven months pregnant, was allegedly beaten to death with a wooden stick by her husband following a domestic dispute in Uttar Pradesh’s Hardoi district.The woman’s mother-in-law was also injured when she intervened to save her.The incident took place in Myora village under the Bilgram Kotwali area, around 30 km from the Hardoi district headquarters.According to family members, the deceased, identified as Kiran (24), had been married to Vishal (26) for around three years. She was approximately seven months pregnant and also had a one-year-old daughter.Police and family members said Vishal and Kiran had a quarrel at around 4 pm on Tuesday over an issue that is being investigated. The argument reportedly escalated, following which Vishal allegedly picked up a stick and began assaulting Kiran.When Vishal’s mother, Prema, intervened and tried to stop the assault, she was also allegedly beaten and sustained injuries.Neighbours rushed to the spot after hearing the commotion and took the injured Kiran to a Community Health Centre (CHC). However, doctors examined her and declared her dead.Police reached the village after being informed about the incident and took Vishal into custody.The police conducted the necessary proceedings on the body and sent it for post-mortem examination to ascertain the exact cause of death. The woman’s parental family was also informed about the incident.Police said the circumstances leading to the dispute, the sequence of events and other aspects of the case were being examined.Bilgram Kotwali inspector Vijay Kumar said police reached the spot immediately after receiving information and started an investigation. He said the husband had been traced and taken into custody, while further legal action would be taken on the basis of the complaint submitted by the family and the findings of the investigation.The police are also examining the circumstances surrounding the death, including the reason behind the altercation and the allegations made by the deceased woman’s family.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Lucknow | Silver Rate in Lucknow | Bank Holidays in Lucknow | Public Holidays in Lucknow | Lucknow AQI | Weather in Lucknow | Petrol Price in Lucknow | Diesel Price in Lucknow | CNG Price in Lucknow | LPG Price in LucknowStay updated with the latest Lucknow news.
